name: Run and verify laboratory tests
summary: This process turns an accepted specimen into a verified result in the patient's chart. Automated chemistry and hematology lines measure most tests, and middleware rules release most results without a person; medical laboratory technologists review the rest, rerun or dilute samples, make blood films, phone critical values and verify results, with pathologists commenting on abnormal films. Results go to the hospital chart and the provincial laboratory information system. Turnaround for ED and stat tests is the main measure; delays come from queues on the line, held results, blood film backlogs overnight and unreachable caregivers for critical values.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation of about 640 beds with a core laboratory running chemistry, immunoassay and hematology automation, stat laboratories at the smaller sites and microbiology referred out.
baseline.notes: One case is one reported test. Daily quality control, maintenance, calibration, proficiency testing and inventory are not case work and are left out of step minutes; they explain part of the stated FTE.

trigger: An accepted specimen is loaded on the analyser line or delivered to a bench.
end_state: The verified result is in the chart and OLIS (with any critical value phoned), or the test is cancelled and a new specimen requested.

volume.seasonality: Higher in winter respiratory season and from 2020 to 2022 with COVID-19 admissions; weekday daytime peaks after the early-morning round and outpatient collection.

evidence.note: 2,597,035 tests in 2018/19 (about 216,000 a month) and 3,220,658 in 2021/22 (about 268,000 a month).

surge.cause: Winter respiratory virus season (influenza and RSV; COVID-19 waves from 2020)

evidence.note: Author's estimate linked to the specimen collection surge.

An academic laboratory reported 19.7 billable tests per paid hour; 235,000 tests a month at that rate needs about 11,900 paid hours, roughly 70 to 75 FTE across all laboratory staff. The organisation file lists 100 technologists (headcount, including part-time and transfusion staff); about 70 FTE on core testing is the author's estimate.
Author's estimate: film and abnormal result review is a small part of the six pathologists' work, most of which is surgical pathology.
Author's estimate: occurrence review and oversight of core testing.

systems.name: Automated chemistry and hematology analyser lines with middleware
Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Ontario Laboratories Information System and ConnectingOntario viewer
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones
Safety incident and complaints reporting system

resources.name: Core laboratory chemistry and hematology analyser lines

steps.name: Route specimen by test and priority
steps.description: Once a tube is on the line, the middleware reads the barcode, looks up the ordered tests in the laboratory information system and routes the tube to the chemistry, immunoassay, hematology or coagulation analyser, flagging stat priority and diverting tests run on a manual bench or in a scheduled batch.

next.condition: routine test on an automated analyser
stat test (ED, ICU, OR or stat inpatient)
test run in a scheduled batch

evidence.note: Author's estimate of the test mix for a community hospital core laboratory with chemistry and hematology automation; microbiology is referred out.

steps.name: Analyser measures the test
steps.description: The analyser aspirates the sample, runs the assay and sends the result with its instrument flags, hemolysis, icterus and lipemia indices and quality control status to the middleware. Waiting time covers the queue on the line and the assay time.

evidence.note: In an Ontario ED, excessive queue and instrument times were identified as causes of delay for potassium, whose order-to-result time was 49 minutes; the queue and assay minutes here are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Apply autoverification rules
steps.description: The middleware compares the result with the laboratory's rules: instrument error flags, interference indices, delta check against the patient's previous result, manual review limits and absurd values. Results that pass are released without a person; the rest are held on the technologist's review screen.

next.condition: passes all rules and is auto-verified

evidence.note: An academic core chemistry laboratory reached 99.5% autoverification, and delta checks or manual review limits prevent autoverification (krasowski2014). The 85% overall rate blends high chemistry rates with much lower hematology rates and no autoverification for manual tests, the author's estimate for a community laboratory in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Technologist reviews held result
steps.description: The medical laboratory technologist opens the held result on the middleware screen, reads the flag, compares it with the patient's previous results and diagnosis in the information system and decides whether to release, rerun, dilute, make a blood film or query the specimen.

error.defect_description: Technologist releases a result that should have been held (for example, an unrecognised interference).

control.basis: Medical laboratory technologists are regulated under the Medical Laboratory Technology Act, 1991 (CMLTO); IQMH accreditation requirements for result review

next.condition: hematology flag needs a blood film
delta check failure; check history and call the unit
suspected analyser or quality control problem

evidence.note: Branch shares are the author's estimate for a community laboratory; the review itself is a professional judgment by a regulated technologist.

steps.name: Rerun or dilute the sample
steps.description: The technologist pulls the tube from the line storage, makes a manual or on-board dilution or reruns the test on the same or the backup analyser, then waits for the repeat result to compare with the first.

next.condition: repeat result confirms or replaces the first

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Make blood film and manual differential
steps.description: For a hematology flag, the technologist makes and stains a blood film (or loads it on the slide maker), examines it under the microscope, counts and classifies cells and enters the manual differential and morphology comments.

error.defect_description: Cell misclassified on the manual differential.

next.condition: abnormal cells; film sent for pathologist review

evidence.note: Author's estimate of film times; slide review queues grow overnight when one technologist covers the bench.

steps.name: Pathologist reviews film or abnormal result
steps.description: The pathologist reviews the flagged film or abnormal result, compares it with the clinical history and earlier results, adds an interpretive comment and, for a new leukemia or other urgent finding, phones the responsible physician.

control.basis: Pathologist interpretation required for abnormal peripheral blood films under the laboratory's IQMH-accredited procedures

evidence.note: Author's estimate: pathologists cover the laboratory on weekdays and by call at other times, so routine films wait for the next working day.

steps.name: Investigate delta check failure
steps.description: When a result differs sharply from the patient's last one, the technologist checks the chart for transfusion, dialysis or a new diagnosis and phones the unit to confirm the collection; an unexplained change suggests a wrong-blood-in-tube error.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Cancel result and request recollection
steps.description: The technologist cancels the result with a coded reason such as 'hemolysed, please recollect' or 'specimen identity in doubt', which shows on the chart, and phones the unit or ED to ask for a new specimen.

evidence.note: When interference limits are exceeded, results may be reported as hemolysed, lipemic or icteric without a value (krasowski2014); the timing is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Verify and release result manually
steps.description: After review, rerun, film or pathologist comment, the technologist enters any comments and verifies the result, which releases it from the laboratory information system.

control.basis: Result verification by a regulated medical laboratory technologist (Medical Laboratory Technology Act, 1991)

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Post result to chart and OLIS
steps.description: The laboratory information system sends the verified result to the patient's chart in the hospital information system, where it shows on the ED tracking board or results screen, and to the Ontario Laboratories Information System; copies go to the family physician.

next.condition: OLIS or chart interface rejects the result

evidence.note: Critical value share and interface error share are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Phone critical value with read-back
steps.description: For a critical result such as a potassium above 6.5 or a hemoglobin below 60, the technologist phones the patient's nurse or physician, gives the result, asks for read-back and records the name, time and read-back in the laboratory information system.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada and IQMH requirements for timely notification of critical results with read-back

next.condition: caregiver not reached on the first call

evidence.note: CAP Q-Probes: critical results were called a median of 4 minutes after the result was known in the laboratory and 56 minutes after collection; read-back was given in a very high percentage of calls; calls through ward clerks were less reliable.

steps.name: Escalate unreachable critical value
steps.description: If no licensed caregiver answers, the technologist pages the charge nurse, the most responsible physician or the on-call physician through switchboard, repeats the calls and documents each attempt until a caregiver accepts the result.

evidence.note: A small share of calls were abandoned; one author insisted that a licensed caregiver be reached eventually. Escalation times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Troubleshoot analyser and quality control
steps.description: When held results suggest a shift, the technologist checks quality control runs, recalibrates or replaces reagent, calls the vendor or biomedical engineering if needed, and reruns the patient samples tested since the last acceptable control.

control.basis: IQMH accreditation requirements for quality control and corrective action before patient results are released

evidence.note: Author's estimate; minutes are for the troubleshooting episode attributed to the held test.

steps.name: Perform manual bench test
steps.description: The technologist performs tests not on the automated line, such as urine microscopy, body fluid cell counts, ESR or a manual coagulation assay, reading results by microscope or instrument and typing them into the laboratory information system.

error.defect_description: Transcription error typing a manual result.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Expedite stat tube
steps.description: The technologist on the stat bench watches the priority lane and the ED pending list, makes sure stat tubes are sampled ahead of routine work and chases tubes that have been received but have no result after the expected time.

evidence.note: Order processing time and queues for potassium delayed ED results; 43% of ED tests were for admitted patients still in the ED. Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Investigate error found after release
steps.description: When a clinician queries a result or the laboratory finds a wrong patient, unit or calculation after release, the technologist pulls the specimen and records, repeats the test if possible and identifies every affected result.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Issue corrected report and notify clinician
steps.description: The technologist amends the result with a corrected-report comment, which flags the change in the chart and OLIS, and phones the responsible physician so that any treatment based on the wrong value can be reviewed.

control.basis: IQMH requirements for amended reports and notification of the ordering physician

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Manager reviews occurrence
steps.description: The laboratory manager reviews the occurrence report, interviews the staff involved, records root cause and corrective action in the incident system and, for harm events, reports to the quality and risk department.

control.basis: IQMH occurrence management requirements; Accreditation Canada patient safety incident management

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Fix rejected interface message and resend
steps.description: A senior technologist works the interface error queue: corrects a health card number or name mismatch, maps a new test code or re-links the ordering physician, then resends the result to the chart or OLIS.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: interface queues are worked on weekdays.

steps.name: Hold test for scheduled batch run
steps.description: Low-volume tests such as protein electrophoresis, some drug levels and special chemistry are stored and run in a batch once a day or a few times a week to save reagent and calibration.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Hematology flag needing a blood film
exceptions.description: A CBC with an abnormal flag waits for a film and manual differential; a share goes on to the pathologist, adding hours to days for routine samples.

exceptions.name: Critical value caregiver not reached
exceptions.description: The technologist cannot reach the nurse or physician on the first call and escalates through the charge nurse or on-call physician.

exceptions.name: Suspected wrong blood in tube
exceptions.description: An unexplained delta check failure leads to cancelling the result and requesting a new sample.

exceptions.name: Corrected report
exceptions.description: An error found after release leads to an amended result, a call to the physician and a manager review.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from specimen on the line to verified result
benchmarks.population: All tests in a community hospital core laboratory

evidence.note: Author's estimate: an Ontario ED measured 49 minutes from order to potassium result and 18 minutes for hemoglobin (fernandes2004), which includes collection and transport, so the laboratory part of a typical test is about 20 to 35 minutes; batched and film-reviewed tests form the tail.
Hemoglobin 18 minutes.
Up from 40% in 2000.

benchmarks.unit: median minutes from result known to call

evidence.note: Median 56 minutes from collection to call.

pain_points.description: ED results are slowed by queues on the line and by the volume of tests for admitted patients boarding in the ED.

evidence.note: Order processing, queue and instrument time for potassium and 43% of ED tests for admitted patients.

pain_points.description: Hematology results that need a film wait for a technologist at the microscope, and abnormal films wait for a pathologist on the next working day.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Critical value calls go to ward clerks or to physicians who are no longer responsible, needing second calls.
Hemolysed samples drawn in the ED produce results that are suppressed and must be recollected.

evidence.note: Interference flags lead to results reported without a value.

assumptions: One case is one reported test; a tube often carries several tests that move together, so the per-test minutes are small shares of shared work.
Microbiology and most special testing are referred to Public Health Ontario or reference laboratories and are outside this process.

Overall autoverification of 85% is lower than the best academic chemistry figure because hematology, coagulation and manual tests autoverify less often; community laboratories in 2019-2022 varied widely.

Daily quality control, maintenance, calibration, proficiency testing, inventory and the transfusion bench are not modelled as case steps; they account for the gap between the touch-time FTE and the stated 70 technologist FTE.
System steps carry no touch time; queue and assay time are in the wait before the analyser step (s02).
The touch-time check implies about 51 FTE against 71 stated, a gap explained by quality control, maintenance and other non-case work.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file; the director of diagnostic services, listed for this process in the organisation file, takes no part in individual tests.
